Des couvertures médiatiques qui divisent: Media coverage that divides, yet again
On ne peut plus se permettre de se cache: We can no longer afford to hide behind the wall of objectivity.
Le journalisme perd de son lustre. N’est: Journalism is losing its lustre. Isn’t it time we started thinking about how we cover the news? Are we empathetic enough toward the public? Beyond Facebook’s algorithms, do we bear some responsibility for the current social climate? When we talk about the N-word in terms of academic freedom, without mentioning the trauma it causes Black people, that’s a choice. When we talk about cultural appropriation without mentioning why it is problematic for the people who denounce it, that’s a choice.
Lorsqu’on présente <l1>un homme noir acc: When we present <l1>a Black man accused of a crime with a mugshot </l1>and a white man accused of a crime in his hot tub or at his graduation, that’s a choice. When we present a suspect as guilty before he has even been tried and reveal details of his personal life, that’s a choice. When we call the perpetrator of the Quebec City attack a killer and not a terrorist, that’s a choice. When we call that tragedy a massacre and not an attack, that’s a choice. When we present three people as the representatives of an entire community, that’s a choice. When we label an anthropologist, a social entrepreneur and a psychosocial worker as activists, that’s a choice.
Lorsqu’on invite quatre hommes blancs à: When we invite four white men to talk about racial profiling, that’s a choice. When we ask a politician in an interview how her love life is going, or when we introduce a woman politician by talking instead about <l1>her heels and her haircut</l1>, that’s a choice. When we decide to once again use photos of Asian people to illustrate the COVID-19 pandemic, that’s a choice. In short, our journalistic choices of photos, angles, quotes, framing and subjects have the power to build perceptions.
Pour plusieurs personnes racisées, autoc: For many racialized, Indigenous, poor or marginalized people, the media coverage they receive contributes to division and does not foster understanding. Through our coverage, we bear a responsibility for social cohesion and for societal tensions.
Malgré toutes nos bonnes intentions, les: Despite all our good intentions, the biases of our newsrooms hurt too many communities. These biases, often unconscious, are something I’ve been collecting since I started studying journalism, when I created a folder on my computer on the subject that has never stopped growing. Today, I use it for my presentations on media bias, but it only takes a few clicks to find more recent examples online. At every presentation I give at my talks, I see journalists’ astonishment. The concepts I talk about aren’t taught in classrooms or in newsrooms.
Pourtant, des cours sur les biais médiat: Yet several reports have recommended courses on media bias and on covering Indigenous issues and visible and cultural minorities: the Bouchard-Taylor report in 2008, the Truth and Reconciliation report in 2015, the Viens Commission report in 2019 and the report of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls in 2019. Yet the implementation of these recommendations is still awaited.
Et on voit aujourd’hui les conséquences: And today we see the consequences of this delay. But at the most basic level, no one bothers to teach journalists the consequences of their choices for the social climate and for political decisions. To me, it is clear that until we commit to making journalism an anti-oppressive tool, we will not be able to resolve this crisis of trust. None of this is new, and things may change with time, but how many lives will have to be lost or upended before we start asking ourselves about the consequences of our choices and our biases?
On ne peut plus se permettre de se cache: We can no longer afford to hide behind the wall of objectivity. Journalistic objectivity does not reflect everyone’s reality. It must be understood through the reality of people whose lives are marginalized. It is with these concerns in mind that I decided to create La Converse. Looking at the columns and media coverage of some of my colleagues, I was so appalled that I couldn’t see myself working in Quebec for a media outlet I could be proud of, whose offices I could walk into with my head held high every morning.
En attendant que les mentalités changent: While waiting for mindsets to change, I decided to take matters into my own hands so as to keep a realistic sense of hope: I created a media outlet built on dialogue and reconciliation. A media outlet where people’s stories are respected, where we take the time to think about the consequences of our actions and what they mean for the communities we talk about. A media outlet where, instead of sacrosanct objectivity, we opt for journalistic integrity, transparency and fairness.
Un média qui, au lieu d’alimenter la div: A media outlet that, instead of fuelling division and hatred, bridges gaps. I’m not saying we’re perfect, and I know we still have a long way to go before we become a key player in Quebec’s media landscape, but I can assure you that we question our editorial choices with every story.
Car le journalisme de demain est un jour: Because the journalism of tomorrow is journalism that thinks about the consequences of its choices on the daily lives of the public it serves. So I’m writing you these few lines to ask you a question: how can we serve you better? We want to hear from you.
Où sont, selon vous, nos angles morts ?: Where do you think our blind spots are?
